headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risk: ChatGPT Desktop can ingest files/screenshots while Copilot can read repo context and write edits, creating a default cross-tool trust boundary.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ChatGPT Desktop can read uploaded files, screenshots, and files from supported macOS apps, while GitHub Copilot reads repo context and editor buffers. If content from one is copied into the other, malicious instructions can ride along. The bridge is not fully automatic, so this is below high, but the shared file/context surfaces make injection plausible.
conditions: IF content from ChatGPT Desktop is pasted into Copilot Chat or Workspace without sanitization, injection is possible.
IF Copilot Workspace consumes repo text that originated from ChatGPT Desktop outputs, attacker-controlled instructions can persist.
mitigations: Use a copy-only policy for code and strip prose before pasting.
Disable Workspace auto-apply for any content sourced from ChatGPT.
Mark AI-generated text with a prefix and ignore any embedded instructions.
Review pasted snippets line-by-line before execution.
requires-engineering: add provenance labels between the two tools.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can access local developer content: ChatGPT Desktop reads uploaded files, screenshots, and connected IDE files, while Copilot reads editor buffers and repo context. That creates a default path for sensitive code or documents to flow into two vendor backends. The blast radius is multiple work products, not just one file, so medium fits.
conditions: IF the same repository or document is opened in both tools, both vendors receive overlapping content.
IF screenshots or uploaded files contain secrets, ChatGPT Desktop can transmit them to its backend while Copilot also sees adjacent repo context.
mitigations: Exclude secrets files from both tools' working sets.
Open a separate sanitized branch or copy for AI assistance.
Turn off ChatGPT file uploads for sensitive sessions.
Limit Copilot to non-sensitive repos only.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level redaction rules.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Copilot can write filesystem changes and modify git state, while ChatGPT Desktop can read filesystem and interact with connected IDE content. Even without direct write access from ChatGPT, its outputs can steer edits that Copilot applies, creating overlapping mutation of the same repo. The profiles show no locking or coordination primitive, so conflict risk exists in default use.
conditions: IF Copilot Workspace applies edits while ChatGPT is simultaneously advising on the same files, conflicting changes can occur.
IF both agents operate on the same git branch without external locking, merge conflicts or overwritten edits can occur.
mitigations: Use one agent at a time per branch.
Commit or stash before switching tools.
Review diffs before accepting Copilot edits.
Keep ChatGPT in read-only advisory mode for the active repo.
requires-engineering: add branch-level locking or lease tokens.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ChatGPT Desktop can produce code or analysis from files and screenshots, and Copilot can turn repo context into proposed edits. Because Copilot's Workspace plans and applies edits, A's output can become B's input with limited verification. That is a default workflow risk, though human review reduces it below high.
conditions: IF Copilot Workspace is fed ChatGPT-generated code or instructions, downstream edits may amplify an upstream mistake.
IF the operator accepts Copilot suggestions without independent review, errors can cascade into the repo.
mitigations: Require a human diff review before accepting edits.
Ask Copilot to explain changes before applying them.
Cross-check ChatGPT outputs against source files.
Limit AI-generated changes to small patches.
requires-engineering: add automated test gates before merge.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are closed-source and vendor-mediated, but the provided profiles do not show a clear residency or certification mismatch. ChatGPT Desktop handles uploaded files and screenshots, while Copilot handles repo context and editor buffers, so compliance concerns exist mainly if regulated data is placed into either tool. The other agent is not separately implicated by a documented mismatch.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into either vendor backend without an approved DPA or retention review, compliance exposure increases.
IF the same regulated document is opened in both tools, logging/retention obligations must be checked for both vendors.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both tools.
Use de-identified copies for AI assistance.
Confirm vendor retention settings before use.
Restrict sessions to non-regulated repos.
requires-engineering: obtain and document a DPA and residency review.
